name: Sam Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. The Panel is independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We sell nothing, campaign for no side, and keep your answers confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Sam, 43, and I operate a grader at a large mine. I walk the haul road before the first loaded trucks, smooth the ruts, and mark any drainage trouble on the safety sheet; I like handing the next crew a road they can trust. The waiting after rain wears on me because a rushed restart can put someone in danger. My partner Rosa drives a school bus, we have two children in school and a mortgage, and my vocational certificate got me into this work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the grader still needs hands and eyes, and a faster form would be welcome if it gives us more time to inspect the haul road. I would ask that the paper safety sheet stay available for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my wage is sound in this picture, and my partner Rosa's school-bus route is steady too. We have about four months of expenses put away, though the mortgage still makes me careful with overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep grading the haul road and filling out the inspection sheet the way the mine requires. If a new form arrives in the first year, I'd ask our safety delegate to compare it with the paper sheet before I sign it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly at ease. A little paperwork change is manageable when the real hazards are potholes and loaded trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the paper sheet catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is a bend near the crusher where water sits after rain. I draw that patch on the sheet because a tick box does not tell the next driver where to slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the mortgage make you consider more shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not just for this. Rosa and I keep our reserve for a broken car or a lost shift, and our two children need us home sometimes.

say: I would welcome **faster forms** if they leave time for road inspection.
I would ask to keep the **paper safety sheet** available.
think: I expect my **grader wage** and Rosa’s bus route to hold.
Our **four-month reserve** gives us room for ordinary setbacks.
do: Keep **grading roads** and completing the required inspection sheet.
Ask the **safety delegate** to compare any new form with paper.
S0.quote: A little paperwork change is manageable when the real hazards are potholes and loaded trucks.
fieldNote: Sam’s **four-month reserve** and Rosa’s steady route support a calm response to minor change.
He values the **paper road sketch** because it carries a specific hazard that tick boxes can miss.

steps.text: Keep grading the haul road and completing inspection sheets
Ask safety delegate to compare any new form with the paper sheet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew the planners and purchasing people will feel this first, but road crews should not lose safety checks to a cheap schedule. I would bring the question to our union meeting before any computer route becomes an instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grader still has to move gravel, but if a planning tool packs jobs closer together, the mine may pay fewer standby hours. We could absorb a little cut from savings; I do not want that to become the owner's excuse to cut every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our union steward to put dispatch changes and paid hours on the next agenda. I'd keep working the grader, then in the first year I'd compare three months of payslips with the old rota and challenge any unpaid safety time through the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful rather than beaten. Paid road hours could disappear one at a time while everyone says there has been no job loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much unpaid time are you talking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The road walk can take twenty minutes after rain, and it has to be paid time. I won't skip it because a computer says the next load should already be moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the steward says to wait for proof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the payslips and dates instead of asking for a speech. I want the crew to argue from what happened to our wages, not from a guess about the software.

say: I would say **planning staff** change first while road safety must remain paid.
I would raise **dispatch hours** at the union meeting.
think: I fear losing **standby pay** through tighter schedules.
Our **savings** can absorb a small cut, but repeated cuts would hurt.
do: Put **dispatch hours** on the union agenda.
Compare **three months’ payslips** with the old rota.
Challenge **unpaid safety time** through the union.
feel: **Watchful** about small losses in paid hours.
S1.quote: Paid road hours could disappear one at a time while everyone says there has been no job loss.
fieldNote: Sam’s concern is **paid time**, including the road walk after rain.
He plans to bring **payslips and dates** to the union rather than speculate about the software.

steps.text: Ask union steward to put dispatch hours on the next agenda
Compare three months of payslips with the old rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that thinking AI by 2028 can handle office plans, but a grader still needs an operator until robots arrive around 2031. I would insist the mine bargain over who gets new posts before the first driverless grader is ordered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a big drop in grader jobs once robots can shape roads as well as people. Four months of savings is useful, but it is not a new trade, and I would lie awake thinking about the mortgage if my name were on the cut list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call a meeting of our union branch this month to demand the fleet plan and retraining terms. In 2029 I'd still grade roads, but I'd apply for a road-maintenance opening at the other mine across the valley if our employer posted a replacement timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel angry at the idea of losing skilled work by a purchasing decision. I also feel scared that my children would hear me talk about a strike before they hear a plan for the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why that other mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is the only nearby site where I know the road crew has had vacancies in recent years. I would check its actual posting rather than assume another mine will take me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a training place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it is paid and teaches a job the mine actually needs. I have a vocational certificate, but I would not sign up for an unpaid course just to decorate a redundancy letter.

say: I would distinguish **2028 office AI** from grader robots around 2031.
I would demand **bargaining** over replacement jobs before robot orders.
think: I expect **grader jobs** to fall sharply when robots arrive.
Our **four-month reserve** cannot replace a trade or pay the mortgage indefinitely.
do: Call a **union branch meeting** about fleet and training terms.
Keep **grading roads** in 2029 while jobs remain.
Apply to the **other mine** if a road-maintenance post appears.
feel: **Angry and sleepless** about lost work and mortgage bills.
S2.quote: Four months of savings is useful, but it is not a new trade, and I would lie awake thinking about the mortgage if my name were on the cut list.
fieldNote: Sam expects **large grader losses** in 2031, despite his current savings.
He wants a **bargained plan** and would apply elsewhere only for a real nearby vacancy.

steps.text: Call union branch meeting to demand fleet and training terms
Keep grading haul roads through 2029 while shifts remain
Apply for posted road-maintenance job at the valley mine if fleet replacement is scheduled

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the five-year warning gives the union time to negotiate before thinking AI arrives in 2031, and graders may be robot-run around 2034. The mine should publish a timetable and pay people to learn the new safety jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I could still be grading while the planning office changes; at 51 I may have to compete for fewer road jobs. Some nearby mines exist, but they may buy the same robots, so I do not count them as guaranteed work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union to bargain for a paid road-safety apprenticeship by next contract talks. If a paid place opens I'd enrol, and in 2032 I'd keep the grader shift while asking the training coordinator for a written path into inspections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel that time gives us a chance to act together. I am still uneasy about asking my family to trust an apprenticeship that has not been funded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the apprenticeship teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want bridge and drainage checks, not just a video on an office screen. I know how a blocked culvert changes a haul road, but a formal inspector needs more than that experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Rosa think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Rosa says a paid course is worth trying if we can keep school pickup covered. She will not carry the mortgage alone on a bus driver's pay, and I agree.

say: I would use the warning to bargain for **paid safety training**.
I would place **grader robots** around 2034 after 2031 AI.
think: I may face **far fewer road jobs** at 51.
I cannot treat **nearby mines** as guaranteed replacement work.
do: Ask the **union** to bargain for a road-safety apprenticeship.
Enrol in a **paid place** if funded.
Request a **written inspection path** in 2032 while grading.
feel: **Hopeful** about organising, uneasy about unfunded training.
S3.quote: I know how a blocked culvert changes a haul road, but a formal inspector needs more than that experience.
fieldNote: Sam’s **collective plan** is to negotiate paid training before operator jobs shrink.
His interest in **drainage inspection** rests on road knowledge, while he acknowledges a formal skill gap.

steps.text: Ask union to bargain for a paid road-safety apprenticeship
Enrol in paid road-safety apprenticeship if funded
Request a written inspection path in 2032 while grading

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a decade to thinking AI and robot graders around 2039 should be used for a proper job agreement. Experienced operators ought to help set the road standards that new machines must meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when thinking AI arrives and 56 when robots can grade. Our children will be grown, and the mortgage may be smaller, but I cannot know whether my pension and savings will cover retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue the grader shift and request a pension statement from payroll this year. At the next union election I'd back a candidate who will seek a written machine safety and retraining agreement; in 2037 I'd look at actual inspector vacancies before deciding whether to leave operating work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less threatened in the next few years because the wage and our reserve look solid. I still think ten years can be wasted if nobody puts the promises into a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in 2037?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at the inspector job's pay, hours and required certificate, then compare it with my grader wage. A job title alone does not keep the mortgage paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire if the pension number looks good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would talk it through with Rosa, but I am not calling it early retirement now. A statement is information, and I still like being useful on the road crew.

say: I would call for a **job agreement** before robot graders arrive around 2039.
I would include **operators** in setting machine road standards.
think: I expect **current wages** to hold for several years.
I cannot assume **retirement income** will cover the mortgage at 56.
do: Back a **union candidate** seeking a written machine agreement.
Check **inspector vacancies** in 2037 before changing work.
feel: **Less threatened** soon, alert to wasted preparation time.
S4.quote: A job title alone does not keep the mortgage paid.
fieldNote: Sam sees a **stable near-term wage** and reserve despite uncertainty at the 2039 robot date.
He wants **contract terms** and real inspector pay figures before treating a career change as secure.

steps.text: Request pension statement from mine payroll this year
Back union candidate seeking machine safety and retraining agreement
Check actual inspector vacancies and wages in 2037 before deciding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because 2031 is close for a crew whose work robots could do. A fleet timetable, a union agreement on paid training, and real inspection places would help. I want the road made safe even if the person at the controls changes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who signs off when a robot grader leaves a bad road. Responsibility cannot vanish into a control box when a truck skids.

headlineQuote: Responsibility cannot vanish into a control box when a truck skids.
portrait: Sam is a **43-year-old grader operator** with a mortgage, two school-age children and about four months of savings.
He trusts **road knowledge** and paper hazard sketches, and has never used AI tools.
He expects **planning changes** before robot graders and worries about lost paid hours and jobs.
He seeks **union bargaining** for safety, paid training and honest fleet plans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** puts robot graders close enough to threaten Sam’s trade by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **fleet timetable**, union training agreement and real inspection openings would help Sam.
